title: How Does Wi-Fi Work?
sources: Cisco, '20 Myths of Wi-Fi Interference' (microwave ovens emit interference in the 2.4 GHz band)
ScienceABC, 'Do Microwaves Interfere With WiFi Signals?' (ovens run near 2.45 GHz; only 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi is affected; 5 GHz is faster with shorter range)
TinkerTry, '2.4 GHz versus 5 GHz WiFi with microwave interference' (5 GHz has smaller range and passes walls less well)
Wi-Fi Alliance / IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi carries digital data on radio waves in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands; a 2.4 GHz wave oscillates about 2.4 billion times per second)

lines.text: Well, your router is plugged into the internet with a cable,
and it turns that data into invisible radio waves.
Those waves carry ones and zeros,
riding on a wave that wiggles billions of times every second.
lines.caps: RIDING A *WAVE | THAT *WIGGLES | *BILLIONS OF TIMES | EVERY *SECOND

lines.text: Your phone's tiny antenna catches them and turns them back into data.
Most routers use two bands, two point four and five gigahertz.
Two point four reaches farther through walls,
while five is faster, but it gets blocked more easily.
And here's the weird part: your microwave uses that same two point four band,
so heating up leftovers can actually slow down your Wi-Fi.
So if it ever lags, check the kitchen.
